title: Stealing work and sizing the threshold

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Per this page, which tasks does an idle ForkJoinPool worker steal from a busy worker's deque, and why those?

options.text: The newest tasks, since they are smaller and still warm in the stealer's cache
options.says: The page says the owning thread takes the newest tasks for cache locality; the stealer takes from the other end.

options.text: The oldest tasks, since they are larger and closer to the root of the tree
options.says: The page says a stealing thread takes older tasks from the bottom, which are larger and closer to the root, so fewer steals are needed.

options.text: A task picked at random, since that spreads the work evenly across the deque
options.says: The page describes a fixed order: the owner works LIFO from the top and the stealer FIFO from the bottom, not a random pick.

questions.stem: Per this page, what goes wrong when a fork/join task's threshold is too small?

options.text: Too few tasks are created, so some cores sit idle
options.says: The page says this is what happens when the threshold is too large, not too small.

options.text: The pool rejects tasks that fall below its minimum size
options.says: The page's threshold-of-1 example runs to completion, creating about two million tasks; nothing is rejected.

options.text: Too many tasks are created, so scheduling overhead dominates
options.says: The page says a threshold that is too small creates too many tasks, and the scheduling overhead dominates.

concepts: A threshold that is too small creates so many tasks that scheduling overhead dominates, and one too large leaves cores idle.
A worker pops its own newest tasks, while an idle worker steals the oldest, larger tasks from the other end of a busy worker's deque.
